                                   4                                 UNITED STATES DISTRICT COURT

                                   5                             NORTHERN DISTRICT OF CALIFORNIA

                                   6                                    SAN FRANCISCO DIVISION

                                   7

                                   8     JEFFERIES FUNDING LLC,                            Case No. 24-cv-05639-TLT (PHK)

                                   9                    Plaintiff,                         ORDER RE: MOTION FOR
                                                                                           SANCTIONS AND ATTORNEYS’ FEES
                                  10             v.
                                                                                           Re: Dkt. No. 205
                                  11     DASAGROUP HOLDINGS CORP., et al.,
                                  12                    Defendants.
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13

                                  14                                               INTRODUCTION

                                  15          Before the Court is Plaintiff Jefferies Funding LLC’s (“Jefferies”) Motion for Sanctions

                                  16   pursuant to Local Rules 7-8 and 37-4 and Fed. R. Civ. P. 37. [Dkt. 205]. Plaintiff seeks monetary

                                  17   sanctions against Defendant Dasagroup Holdings Corp. (“Dasagroup”) to compensate Plaintiff for

                                  18   fees incurred in relation to the 30(b)(6) deposition of Dasagroup’s corporate representative Mr.

                                  19   Philip Ward noticed for November 24, 2025. [Dkt. 205]. The requested sanctions include travel

                                  20   costs, court reporter fees and the videographer cancellation fees incurred as a result of Dasagroup’s

                                  21   conduct. Id. Additionally, Plaintiff seeks fees associated with bringing the Motion for Sanctions.

                                  22   Id. The Court held a hearing on the instant motion on April 9, 2026, during which the disputes here

                                  23   were narrowed as discussed below. [Dkt. 222].

                                  24                                               BACKGROUND

                                  25          Jefferies is a Delaware limited liability company specializing in investment banking and

                                  26   capital markets firm. [Dkt. 1 (Complaint) at ¶ 12]. Dasagroup is a Washington corporation

                                  27   specializing in avocado buying and selling. [Dkt. 28 (Amended Counterclaim) at ¶¶ 2, 8]. Mr.

                                  28   Philip Ward is Dasagroup’s President and a named individual co-defendant who was added to the
                                        Case 3:24-cv-05639-TLT           Document 283          Filed 08/05/26     Page 2 of 12




                                   1   case as a named defendant by the First Amended Complaint filed on August 6, 2025. See Dkt. 1;

                                   2   Dkt. 122.

                                   3           On September 17, 2025, Dasagroup’s then counsel, the Moya Law Firm, moved to withdraw

                                   4   as Dasagroup’s counsel. [Dkt. 147]. Because a corporate entity cannot proceed pro se, on

                                   5   November 4, 2025, Judge Thompson ordered Dasagroup “to secure counsel no later than November

                                   6   21, 2025.” [Dkt. 178].

                                   7           Individually, Defendant Ward failed to promptly retain counsel to represent him and

                                   8   proceeded pro se for several months. After a Case Management Conference held on October 23,

                                   9   2025, the presiding District Judge’s Minute Order directed “Mr. Ward to find new counsel no later

                                  10   than 11/12/2025. All previously ordered dates are maintained.” [Dkt. 172]. In that regard, the case

                                  11   scheduling order set November 30, 2025 as the deadline for fact discovery. See Dkt. 136.

                                  12           Plaintiff had served the original 30(b)(6) deposition notice on Dasagroup on May 16, 2025.
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13   [Dkt. 205-1 at ¶ 7]. By agreement of the Parties, the deposition was postponed and Plaintiff served

                                  14   an amended deposition notice on October 27, 2025, setting the deposition for November 24, 2025.

                                  15   Id. at ¶ 8. Defendants did not object to this deposition date. Id. On October 30, 2025 (during

                                  16   Defendant Ward’s deposition as an individual), both Defendant Ward and Dasagroup’s then-counsel

                                  17   confirmed they would appear at the 30(b)(6) deposition on November 24. Id. On November 4,

                                  18   2025, Plaintiff served a second amended 30(b)(6) deposition notice which narrowed the topics for

                                  19   Dasagroup’s deposition in light of Mr. Ward’s individual deposition, but did not change the date.

                                  20   Id. at ¶ 9.

                                  21           Defendants repeatedly sought to stay this case. On October 8, 2025, Dasagroup filed an ex

                                  22   parte application to stay the proceedings pending resolution of Defendants’ challenge to subject

                                  23   matter jurisdiction. [Dkt. 162]. Judge Thompson denied that motion on October 20, 2025. [Dkt.

                                  24   171]. On October 27, 2025, Mr. Ward filed an ex parte motion directed to Judge Thompson seeking

                                  25   a protective order to stay or postpone his then-pending deposition. [Dkt. 174]. Judge Thompson

                                  26   denied that motion and reiterated that “[a]ll prior orders remain in full force and effect.” [Dkt. 176].

                                  27   On November 21, 2025, Dasagroup’s then counsel filed a Notice with the Court reporting that

                                  28   Dasagroup “expects to retain new counsel imminently in this case.” [Dkt. 181 at 2]. In that same
                                                                                          2
                                        Case 3:24-cv-05639-TLT           Document 283          Filed 08/05/26   Page 3 of 12




                                   1   Notice, Dasagroup’s counsel renewed the prior request that the Court stay the action and grant a

                                   2   continuance of all deadlines for new counsel to get up to speed on the matter. Id. Facially, that

                                   3   Notice failed to comply with the Civil Local Rules regarding motions for reconsideration and for ex

                                   4   parte applications, and no such stay or continuance was granted.

                                   5          By November 23, 2025, Mr. Ward and Dasagroup failed to retain counsel by the Court-

                                   6   ordered deadlines. On the noticed date of the deposition, Jefferies’s counsel, who had traveled from

                                   7   out-of-state, and Mr. Ward (as 30(b)(6) representative) were present at the deposition location in

                                   8   Seattle. [Dkt. 205-1 at ¶¶ 11-13]. That morning, Dasagroup’s then-counsel informed Plaintiff’s

                                   9   counsel that new counsel for Dasagroup had been retained, Attorney Dosa. Id. at ¶ 11. As of the

                                  10   date of the deposition, Dasagroup’s then-counsel (Mr. Moya) was still counsel of record for

                                  11   Dasagroup and the new counsel, Attorney Dosa, had not yet entered appearance. Id. Attorney Dosa

                                  12   contacted Plaintiff’s counsel at the time the deposition was set to start, stating that he would not
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13   proceed because he was not prepared. Id. at ¶ 12. Because Attorney Dosa was not present, Mr.

                                  14   Ward refused to testify at the deposition. Id. at ¶ 13.

                                  15          Separately, the Parties had stipulated, and the Court ordered, that Mr. Ward would serve

                                  16   substantive amended responses to Jefferies’ First Set of Interrogatories by January 23, 2026. [Dkt.

                                  17   202]. Additionally, this Stipulation and Order required Dasagroup to provide its amended responses

                                  18   to Jefferies’ Requests for Admissions Nos. 1 and 2 by January 23, 2026. Id.

                                  19          On February 5, 2026, Jefferies moved for sanctions arising from Defendants’ failures to

                                  20   provide written discovery responses and Dasagroup’s counsel’s failure to appear at the November

                                  21   24 deposition. See Dkt. 205. As of the filing date of the instant motion, neither Mr. Ward nor

                                  22   Dasagroup had served responses to Jefferies’s and Third-Party Defendant Silo Technologies’

                                  23   written discovery requests. Id. By the date of the hearing on the instant motion (April 9, 2026),

                                  24   however, Dasagroup and Mr. Ward had provided responses to the discovery requests.

                                  25                                              LEGAL STANDARD

                                  26          “The district court has great latitude in imposing sanctions under Fed.R.Civ.P. 37.” Lew v.

                                  27   Kona Hosp., 754 F.2d 1420, 1425 (9th Cir. 1985). Courts “may impose sanctions, including payment

                                  28   of expenses, on a party who fails to appear for his own deposition after receiving proper notice.” Id.
                                                                                          3
                                        Case 3:24-cv-05639-TLT            Document 283           Filed 08/05/26      Page 4 of 12




                                   1   at 1426; see Fed. R. Civ. P. 37(d). “[T]he court must require the party failing to act, the attorney

                                   2   advising that party, or both to pay the reasonable expenses, including attorney's fees, caused by the

                                   3   failure, unless the failure was substantially justified or other circumstances make an award of

                                   4   expenses unjust.” Fed. R. Civ. P. 37(d)(3).

                                   5           The “customary method” for awarding fees is the lodestar method, calculated by multiplying

                                   6   the number of hours reasonably expended by the prevailing party in the litigation by a “reasonable

                                   7   hourly rate.” Hiken v. Dep’t of Defense, 836 F.3d 1037, 1044 (9th Cir. 2016) (quoting Morales v.

                                   8   City of San Rafael, 96 F.3d 359, 363 (9th Cir. 1996)). “There is a ‘strong presumption’ that the

                                   9   lodestar figure represents a reasonable award.” Id. (citation omitted). “It is axiomatic that ‘trial

                                  10   courts need not, and indeed should not, become green-eyeshade accountants’ in examining fee

                                  11   requests since ‘[t]he essential goal in shifting fees (to either party) is to do rough justice, not to

                                  12   achieve auditing perfection.’” Elec. Priv. Info. Ctr. v. Nat’l Sec. Agency, 87 F. Supp. 3d 223, 235
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13   (D.D.C. Apr. 8, 2015) (quoting Fox v. Vice, 563 U.S. 826, 838 (2011)). A lodestar figure should

                                  14   only be departed from “if certain factors relating to the nature and difficulty of the case overcome

                                  15   this strong presumption and indicate that such an adjustment is necessary.” Hiken, 836 F.3d at 1044

                                  16   (citing Long v. U.S. I.R.S., 932 F.2d 1309, 1314 (9th Cir. 1991)).

                                  17           The district court must “provide a . . . detailed account of how it arrives at appropriate figures

                                  18   for ‘the number of hours reasonably expended’ and ‘a reasonable hourly rate.’” Hiken, 836 F.3d at

                                  19   1044 (quoting Blum v. Stenson, 465 U.S. 886, 888 (1984)). “Though the district court generally

                                  20   possesses a ‘superior understanding of the litigation,’ ‘[i]t remains important . . . for the district court

                                  21   to provide a concise but clear explanation of its reasons for the fee award.’” Id. (quoting Hensley v.

                                  22   Eckerhart, 461 U.S. 424, 437 (1983)).

                                  23           Once a lodestar figure is determined, it is “presumed to be [a] reasonable fee.” Blum, 465

                                  24   U.S. at 897. “The district court may nonetheless consider other factors in determining whether to

                                  25   adjust the fee award upward or downward,” but it “should explain why the adjustment was

                                  26   appropriate.” Hiken, 836 F.3d at 1044.

                                  27                                                DISCUSSION

                                  28           I.      WITHDRAWAL OF REQUEST FOR EVIDENTIARY SANCTIONS
                                                                                            4
                                        Case 3:24-cv-05639-TLT           Document 283          Filed 08/05/26      Page 5 of 12




                                   1          As noted, Plaintiff’s motion for sanctions originally sought both evidentiary and monetary

                                   2   sanctions.   [Dkt. 205].     The primary grounds for the request for evidentiary sanctions was

                                   3   Dasagroup’s and Defendant Ward’s then-failures to provide the ordered responses to Plaintiff’s

                                   4   written discovery requests, detailed above. By the time of the hearing on the instant motion,

                                   5   however, both Dasagroup and Mr. Ward had served responses to the discovery requests.

                                   6   Accordingly, Plaintiff withdrew the request for evidentiary sanctions at the hearing. See Dkt. 222.

                                   7          In light of the discussion at the hearing, the Court DENIES AS MOOT Plaintiff’s request

                                   8   for evidentiary sanctions.

                                   9          The Court now turns to Plaintiff’s request for monetary sanctions regarding Defendants’

                                  10   counsel’s failure to appear at the Deposition.

                                  11          II.     MONETARY SANCTIONS

                                  12          Plaintiff requests that the Court impose monetary sanctions, for both the costs and expenses
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13   incurred in connection with the November 24 deposition, as well as for an award of attorneys’ fees

                                  14   associated with the deposition and the instant motion. Under Rule 37, a district court may impose

                                  15   monetary sanctions, including payment of expenses, on a party who fails to appear for their own

                                  16   deposition after receiving proper notice. See Fed. R. Civ. P. 37(d)(1)(a)(i); see also O'Donnell v.

                                  17   Chase Bank USA NA, No. EDCV142074JGBKKX, 2015 WL 12655697, at *2 (C.D. Cal. May 1,

                                  18   2015) (“failure of a party to attend his deposition . . . will subject that party to sanctions under Rule

                                  19   37(d)”).

                                  20          The threshold issue then is whether sanctions should be imposed for the failures associated

                                  21   with the deposition. As detailed above, Defendants’ conduct in the context of the timeline of this

                                  22   case is both undisputed and, as discussed further below, unexcused. In the weeks preceding the

                                  23   deposition, Defendants were well aware of the impending fact discovery deadline (previously set

                                  24   for November 30, 2025). See Dkt. 136 (Revised Case Management and Scheduling Order issued

                                  25   on August 22, 2025). Judge Thompson had also made clear to the Parties (including Defendants)

                                  26   that all court-ordered deadlines were maintained, despite Mr. Ward’s proceeding pro se and despite

                                  27   the then-pending motions. See Dkt. 171 (Order Denying Dasagroup’s Ex Parte Application to Stay

                                  28   Proceedings issued October 20, 2025); Dkt. 172 (Minutes of Further Case Management Conference
                                                                                          5
                                        Case 3:24-cv-05639-TLT          Document 283          Filed 08/05/26     Page 6 of 12




                                   1   stating “All previously ordered dates are maintained.”). None of Defendants’ motions or requests

                                   2   to stay the proceedings in the fall of 2025 were granted, and Judge Thompson repeatedly emphasized

                                   3   that the case schedule would remain in place.

                                   4          As detailed above, Plaintiff originally served the 30(b)(6) deposition notice on Defendants

                                   5   months prior to the deposition date, and served the first amended deposition notice on October 27,

                                   6   2025, approximately one month prior to the noticed deposition date. [Dkt. 205-1 (Durham Decl.)

                                   7   at 3, ¶ 8]. Both Mr. Ward and Dasagroup’s then-counsel confirmed, on October 30, that they would

                                   8   appear at the 30(b)(6) deposition noticed for November 24. As of the date of the deposition,

                                   9   Dasagroup’s prior counsel was still counsel of record for Dasagroup and new counsel had not yet

                                  10   entered appearance. Defendants gave literally day-of, last minute notice to Plaintiff that neither

                                  11   current counsel (Mr. Moya) nor the new counsel (Mr. Dosa) would appear at the Deposition.

                                  12          It is undisputed that Plaintiff incurred travel costs, videographer and court reporter fees, and
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13   unproductive attorney time for the deposition.         Defendants provide neither substantive nor

                                  14   persuasive arguments as to why they delayed giving notice to Plaintiff that their counsel did not

                                  15   intend to appear. Indeed, Defendants’ opposition provides no reasonable excuse for the failure to

                                  16   warn Plaintiff’s counsel that the deposition might not go forward because prior counsel would

                                  17   simply fail to appear (because of the pending motion to withdraw) and new counsel would object to

                                  18   proceeding without the time to prepare and get up to speed on the case. See Dkt. 215. This is

                                  19   especially inexcusable given Mr. Ward’s and prior counsel’s confirmation on October 30 that they

                                  20   would appear at the deposition (just a few weeks later).

                                  21          Further, the timing is suspect. After repeatedly seeking stays of the case, Defendants were

                                  22   faced with the prospect that the deposition would go forward as noticed. Despite explicit directives

                                  23   from Judge Thompson to engage new counsel by a deadline days if not weeks prior to the deposition

                                  24   date, Mr. Ward (on behalf of Dasagroup) finalized the engagement of new counsel on the day before

                                  25   the deposition – which gave no time for that new counsel to enter appearance before the deposition

                                  26   and lent itself to a ready argument that such counsel could not appear because he had not had time

                                  27   to prepare for the deposition. Dasagroup was under express directive from Judge Thompson to

                                  28   engage new counsel by earlier in November, and any reasonable process for finding new counsel
                                                                                         6
                                        Case 3:24-cv-05639-TLT           Document 283         Filed 08/05/26     Page 7 of 12




                                   1   would have required Mr. Ward (as President of Dasagroup) to work on retaining new counsel days

                                   2   if not weeks prior to the Deposition. Both Mr. Ward and the former and current attorneys for

                                   3   Dasagroup should have known days ahead of the deposition that new counsel’s entry into the case

                                   4   would impact the ability of the deposition to go forward. It is indeed inconceivable that they were

                                   5   unaware of the complications with the Deposition at least one day prior to the deposition.

                                   6   Defendants and their counsel (at least then-counsel of record) could have (but failed to) raise the

                                   7   issue with Plaintiff’s counsel before Plaintiff’s counsel had traveled to Seattle, and before the court

                                   8   reporter and videographer showed up at the deposition.

                                   9          All discovery in this case was referred to the undersigned on March 10, 2025. [Dkts. 74-

                                  10   75]. The undersigned’s Standing Discovery Order expressly states that “Counsel shall also comply

                                  11   with the Northern District of California’s Guidelines for Professional Conduct, in particular section

                                  12   9 to 11 of the Court’s Guidelines regarding discovery.” See Standing Discovery Order at Section
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13   A. The Court’s Guidelines for Professional Conduct, in turn, state that “[a] lawyer should (i) notify

                                  14   opposing counsel and, if appropriate, the court as early as possible when scheduled meetings,

                                  15   hearings, or depositions must be cancelled or rescheduled, and (ii) provide alternate dates for such

                                  16   meetings, hearings, or depositions when possible.” See Guideline 3. Here, clearly Defendants’

                                  17   counsel did not notify opposing counsel as early as possible that the 30(b)(6) deposition of

                                  18   Dasagroup would have to be rescheduled, and certainly did not provide alternate dates.

                                  19          In light of the above, the Court finds that monetary sanctions are warranted for Defendants’

                                  20   counsel’s failure to appear at the deposition, failure to warn (until the very day of the deposition)

                                  21   Plaintiff’s counsel prior to the deposition that rescheduling would be required, providing no advance

                                  22   notice of the problems with the deposition (which would have avoided the costs and fees sought

                                  23   here), and for the resulting refusal by Mr. Ward to testify as the 30(b)(6) representative of Dasagroup

                                  24   based on both then-counsel’s failure to appear and new counsel’s inability to appear due to

                                  25   Dasagroup’s delay in finalizing his retention.

                                  26          Therefore, exercising its authority under Rule 37, the Court imposes monetary sanctions on

                                  27   Defendants in the form of an award to Plaintiffs of reasonable attorneys’ fees and costs.

                                  28          III.    REASONABLE ATTORNEY FEES
                                                                                         7
                                        Case 3:24-cv-05639-TLT           Document 283         Filed 08/05/26     Page 8 of 12




                                   1           Here, Plaintiff seeks an award of its attorneys’ fees incurred in connection with the

                                   2   November 24 deposition and with drafting the Motion for Sanctions. The “customary method” for

                                   3   awarding fees is the lodestar method, calculated by multiplying the number of hours reasonably

                                   4   expended by the prevailing party in the litigation by a “reasonable hourly rate.” Hiken, 836 F.3d at

                                   5   1044 (citation omitted). “There is a ‘strong presumption’ that the lodestar figure represents a

                                   6   reasonable award.”      Id. (quoting Long, 932 F.2d at 1314). “The lodestar figure ‘roughly

                                   7   approximates the fee that the prevailing attorney would have received if he or she had been

                                   8   representing a paying client who was billed by the hour in a comparable case,’ and is therefore a

                                   9   presumptively reasonable fee.” Kelly, 822 F.3d at 1099 (quotation cleaned) (citation omitted). The

                                  10   district court must “provide a ... detailed account of how it arrives at appropriate figures for ‘the

                                  11   number of hours reasonably expended’ and ‘a reasonable hourly rate.’” Id. at 1044 (quoting Blum,

                                  12   465 U.S. at 888).
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13                  a. Hourly Rates

                                  14           In order to determine the lodestar, the first step is to determine whether the hourly rates for

                                  15   the Plaintiff’s attorneys are reasonable. A reasonable hourly rate is ordinarily the “prevailing market

                                  16   rate [ ] in the relevant community.” Kelly v. Wengler, 822 F.3d 1085, 1099 (9th Cir. 2016) (quoting

                                  17   Perdue v. Kenny A. ex rel. Winn, 559 U.S. 542, 551 (2010)). In support of its request for fees,

                                  18   Plaintiff seeks an award for the hours spent by three attorneys: Ms. McNeill (a sixth-year associate),

                                  19   Ms. Durham (a seventh-year associate), and Mr. Silivos (a partner) of the law firm representing

                                  20   Plaintiff.

                                  21           Ms. McNeill’s rate is $796 per hour. [Dkt. 218-1 (Durham Reply Decl.) at ¶ 12]. Although

                                  22   she is one year senior, Ms. Durham’s hourly rate is $764 per hour. Id. The rate of Mr. Silivos is

                                  23   $936 per hour. Id. Plaintiff’s counsel avers that these rates are representative of those customarily

                                  24   charged in the San Francisco and New York markets. Id. at ¶ 13. Additionally, both in briefing and

                                  25   at the hearing regarding the instant motion, counsel for Defendants did not object to these hourly

                                  26   rates or argue that they were unreasonable. Finally, these rates are within the range of reasonable

                                  27   and customary rates in the Northern District of California based on the undersigned’s familiarity

                                  28   with hourly rates in this market (based on thirty-two years of experience in private practice prior to
                                                                                         8
                                        Case 3:24-cv-05639-TLT          Document 283          Filed 08/05/26     Page 9 of 12




                                   1   taking the bench).

                                   2          In light of the above factors, the Court finds that each of the rates for these Plaintiff’s

                                   3   attorneys are reasonable.

                                   4                  b. Number of Hours

                                   5          The next step in calculating the lodestar is to determine whether the attorneys at issue spent

                                   6   a reasonable number of hours on the work for which fees are requested. “A district court, using the

                                   7   lodestar method to determine the amount of attorney’s fees to award, must determine a reasonable

                                   8   number of hours for which the prevailing party should be compensated.” Gonzalez v. City of

                                   9   Maywood, 729 F.3d 1196, 1202 (9th Cir. 2013); see, e.g., Fischer v. SJB–P.D. Inc., 214 F.3d 1115,

                                  10   1119 (9th Cir. 2000). “Ultimately, a ‘reasonable’ number of hours equals ‘[t]he number of hours .

                                  11   . . [which] could reasonably have been billed to a private client.’” Gonzalez, 729 F.3d at 1202

                                  12   (quoting Moreno v. City of Sacramento, 534 F.3d 1106, 1111 (9th Cir. 2008). “[T]o determine
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13   whether attorneys for the prevailing party could have reasonably billed the hours they claim to their

                                  14   private clients, the district court should begin with the billing records the prevailing party has

                                  15   submitted. Although opposing counsel’s billing records may be relevant to determining whether

                                  16   the prevailing party spent a reasonable number of hours on the case, those records are not

                                  17   dispositive.” Gonzalez, 729 F.3d at 1202. “In determining the appropriate number of hours to be

                                  18   included in a lodestar calculation, the district court should exclude hours ‘that are excessive,

                                  19   redundant, or otherwise unnecessary.’” McCown v. City of Fontana, 565 F.3d 1097, 1102 (9th Cir.

                                  20   2009) (citation omitted).

                                  21          In support of the instant motion, Plaintiff’s counsel submitted the time entries for each of the

                                  22   attorneys at issue. See Dkt. 218-1 at Exhibit E. At the hearing on the instant motion, Defendants’

                                  23   counsel primarily argued that the number of hours spent by Plaintiff’s counsel on the instant motion

                                  24   are excessive. The Court addresses the hours spent on the work by each attorney in turn.

                                  25                          i. Ms. McNeill’s Hours

                                  26          According to Plaintiff’s time entries, Ms. McNeill (as the most junior attorney on this team)

                                  27   worked a total of 25.3 hours for which fees are requested (which totals $20,138.80 in fees using her

                                  28   hourly billing rate). See Dkt. 218-1 at 35-36 (Exhibit E). The Court notes that Plaintiff’s counsel’s
                                                                                         9
                                        Case 3:24-cv-05639-TLT         Document 283             Filed 08/05/26   Page 10 of 12




                                   1   declaration states that Ms. McNeill worked 26.5 hours, but that number is not reflected when totaling

                                   2   the hours submitted in the specific time entries. See Dkt. 218-1 at ¶ 12; Dkt. 218-1 at 35 (Exhibit

                                   3   E). Accordingly, the Court assumes Plaintiff’s counsel’s declaration contained an inadvertent

                                   4   mathematical or arithmetic error.

                                   5          The time entries reflect that Ms. McNeill spent 0.7 total hours discussing the motion with

                                   6   her colleagues; 0.2 hours corresponding with her team about court reporter and videographer

                                   7   expenses; 13 hours conducting research for the motion, 2.1 hours preparing the motion, discussing

                                   2           In light of Ms. Durham’s experience with litigating commercial matters in federal courts and
